items.title: 10.17.2 Feasibility of a reaction using E standard values

source_refs.note: Topic 10.17.2 with Figures 10.9 and 10.10, printed pages 231-233.

blocks.text: Standard electrode potential values measure how easy or difficult it is to oxidise or reduce a species. The values are listed in order of increasingly negative values, with the more oxidised form on the left and the more reduced form on the right of each half-equation. The more positive the E standard, the greater the tendency of the half-equation to proceed forward and the easier it is to reduce the species on the left; the less positive the E standard, the greater the tendency to proceed in reverse and the easier it is to oxidise the species on the right.

To check the feasibility of a reaction between Mg2+ and Ag we need the half-equations: Mg2+ + 2e- giving Mg, E standard = -2.32 V, and Ag+ + e- giving Ag, +0.80 V. If Mg2+ were reduced and Ag oxidised, E cell = E(reduction) - E(oxidation) = (-2.32) - (+0.80) = -1.52 V; the negative value shows the reaction is not feasible. The reaction between Ag+ and Mg is feasible, since E cell = (-0.80) - (-2.32) = +1.52 V is positive.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book's arithmetic is wrong: (-2.32) - (+0.80) = -3.12 V, not -1.52 V; and for Ag+ with Mg the E standard of Ag+/Ag is +0.80 V, so E cell = (+0.80) - (-2.32) = +3.12 V, not +1.52 V. The conclusions (Mg2+ with Ag not feasible, Ag+ with Mg feasible) are unchanged.

blocks.alt: Six half-equations in order: Cl2 + 2e- to 2Cl-(aq), E = +1.36 V; Ag+(aq) + e- to Ag(s), +0.80 V; Cu2+(aq) + 2e- to Cu(s), +0.34 V; H+(aq) + e- to 1/2 H2(g), +0.00 V; Zn2+(aq) + 2e- to Zn(s), -0.76 V; Mg2+(aq) + 2e- to Mg(s), -2.38 V. An up arrow on the left (oxidizing power of the left side increasing) points to 'Strongest Oxidizing agent'; a down arrow on the right (reducing power of the right side increasing) to 'Strongest Reducing agent'.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.9: Standard electrode potentials for some oxidizing and reducing agents (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.9).

blocks.text: For the Cu2+/Cu and Zn2+/Zn pair, zinc has the greater tendency to lose electrons, so the reaction in that half-cell runs in reverse, Zn giving Zn2+ + 2e-, and the two half-equations combine to Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) giving Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s), the reaction taking place in the cell: zinc metal with copper ions is feasible, and if the forward reaction is feasible the reverse (copper metal with zinc ions) is not. A piece of copper placed in 1.00 mol dm-3 Zn2+ solution does not react. With the half-equations written one above the other, the direction of reaction follows a clockwise pattern (reactant, product, reactant, product) starting from the top left (Figure 10.10): a reaction occurs so that the stronger oxidising agent reacts with the stronger reducing agent.

blocks.alt: An E standard / V arrow points upward, with +0.34 beside the upper line and -0.76 beside the lower. In a box: Cu2+ + 2e- in equilibrium with Cu, Cu2+ labelled Better oxidant (Reactant) and Cu (Product); below it Zn2+ + 2e- in equilibrium with Zn, Zn2+ labelled (Product) and Zn Better reductant (Reactant). A curved arrow runs over the top from Cu2+ to Cu and another under the bottom from Zn to Zn2+, a clockwise pattern.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.10: A reaction occurs in a direction so that the stronger oxidizing agent reacts with the stronger reducing agent (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.10).
